comments.comment: The argument can be sharper here, right? What is the motivation? Why restate the equations? My take is that adam takes an adaptive step, but the diagnostics from the equations X, Y (ref them here) still is very informative about what is happening on the loss landscape. About the curvature, constructive-destructive regimes, etc. we're measuring different points in space between steps. Those are fed into the adaptive optimizer, so they influence the movement. The goal here is to do a qualitative argument and tell the reader why and how the diagnostic we're proposing can help in adam optimization.
comments.selected_text: Although dt determines the step, the raw gradients still reveal variation in local slope along the adaptive trajectory. Their consecutive alignment and magnitudes distinguish directional reversal from a sharp increase in local slope. The first moment shows how this changing input propagates through the optimizer’s memory. The projected-change diagnostic remains exactly com- putable as ηbκt = 1 ∥gt∥ ∥gt−1∥. (27) Under Adam, this is normalized projected raw-gradient change along the realized path; it is not the SGD directional-curvature estimate. A value above two requires negative cosine and a sufficiently large consecutive norm ratio. Thus, reversal and norm growth explain the diagnostic’s increase algebraically, rather than supplying independent confirmations of instability. The reference at two recalls the GD analysis, but does not identify an Adam stability boundary.

comments.selected_text: To examine repetition without selecting on gradients, write Ls := L(θs) for the recorded training loss. Starting at initial- ization, let ai be the earliest available state with Lai+1 > Lai. Hold the pre-rise reference Lai fixed. When a return is observed within T updates, define the first recovery and peak by ci := min{s : ai < s Ls ≤Lai}, pi := min arg max ai<s<ci Ls. (28) An event is included only when recovery is observed by T = 1024. Search resumes at ci; partial declines and additional local maxima before this return belong to the same event. Thus ai is the last pre-rise state, ai + 1 the first elevated state, pi the loss peak, and ci the first recovered state. Peak increase is 100(Lpi/Lai −1); rise and recovery times are pi−ai and ci− pi, in optimizer updates. The three loss ratios are 1, Lpi/Lai and Lci/Lai

comments.selected_text: Figure 7 places the illustrations within the complete distri- bution of recovered excursions. Small fluctuations coexist with long tails; larger rates populate more severe excursions, al- though the distributions overlap and do not undergo a uniform shift. To focus the anatomy analysis on pronounced changes, we retain events with peak increase strictly greater than 10%. This is an operational amplitude filter chosen for interpretation, not a separation inferred from a density minimum or an optimizer stability threshold. The density retains all amplitudes so that the selection remains visible in context. The filtered sample contains 129 recovered events. Two further above- threshold candidates without observed recovery are excluded. For Table II, pre-rise diagnostics are measured at θai, hence use gradient index ai + 1. Recovery entries first average each event’s diagnostic over the arrival states pi + 1, . . . , ci, then summarize those means across events with equal event weight. They are not values only at ci. The norm-ratio columns instead use the endpoints ∥gpi+1∥/∥gai+1∥and ∥gci+1∥/∥gpi+1∥. The gradient norm’s own maximum need not coincide with the loss peak.
